name: Double-breasted suit

image.caption: Double Breasted Checked – Medium Light Grey Glen Check Suit

lead: A double-breasted suit has a jacket whose front overlaps widely and carries two symmetrical columns of buttons, usually with peaked lapels. The extra cloth across the front adds structure and horizontal width to the chest.

It has been popular in two main periods, the mid-1930s to late 1950s and the mid-1980s to early 2000s, and remains a tailoring staple in the UK and with some designers. No studies measure its effect on perceived attractiveness; tailors and style writers describe its silhouette effects.

paras: It is worn as a formal or business suit, typically buttoned on a six-on-two or four-on-one layout with the lower button fastened, often made-to-measure so the overlap sits flat. Wearers who want a broader-looking upper body, or a more formal, classic look, choose it over a single-breasted cut.
No health risks. Sources note that heavier button counts can overwhelm a shorter torso, and that some men on forums dislike the style or advise against it, so fit and occasion are the usual concerns.

angle.text: The cut itself adds visual width and formality at the chest. Wearers use it to make shoulders and torso look fuller, and often pair it with tailoring so the jacket sits close at the waist.

lead: A double-breasted jacket has wide, overlapping front flaps and two symmetrical columns of buttons, where a single-breasted jacket has a narrow overlap and one column. On most modern jackets one column is decorative and the other functional, with an inner anchor button holding the layers together [1].

People use it to look broader in the chest and more formal. The overlapping front and usual peaked lapels create a strong horizontal and V-shaped line across the upper body, which is why it comes up in forum discussions of building a physique-flattering wardrobe [1][2].

The style was normal for frock coats in the 19th century, became popular for suit jackets from the mid-1930s to the late 1950s, and had a second wave from the mid-1980s to the early 2000s. Demand fell in the United States in the mid-2000s while it stayed popular in the UK [1].
infobox: Two columns; common layouts six-on-two, six-on-one, Kent four-on-one [1]
Single-breasted suit, trench coat, Guards coat

paras: Double-breasted jackets are described by total buttons followed by buttons that fasten, as in six-on-two or six-on-one. The Kent, a four-button style fastened only at the lowest button, is named after Prince George, Duke of Kent, who popularised it [1]. Double-breasted jackets fasten left over right, as men's jackets do, and usually have peaked lapels [1].
Style references note that six buttons can overwhelm a shorter torso, and that a four- or six-button version where only the bottom button fastens may suit those builds better [1].

The cut was standard on 19th-century frock coats. Around 1900 early lounge suits were mostly single-breasted, which has been the default since. The double-breasted suit was popular from the mid-1930s through the late 1950s and again from the mid-1980s into the early 2000s; designers such as Joseph Abboud and Ralph Lauren kept producing it afterwards [1]. Overcoats such as the trench and Guards coat are traditionally double-breasted [1].

On T Nation, men discussing suits give mixed views: one poster lists a double-breasted blazer among the pieces a well-dressed man should own [2], while others say they dislike double-breasted jackets [3][4].

lore.intro: T Nation members occasionally debate double-breasted jackets in threads about dressing well [2][3][4].
